name: Charged Shell of Dust
description: A thin spherical shell of charged dust, with flat spacetime inside it and Reissner-Nordström's field outside. Shrunk to a point at rest it is the classical point charge of Richard Arnowitt, Stanley Deser, and Charles Misner, with a finite mass set by its charge alone. Dropped from infinity with more charge than rest mass it falls through both horizons, turns round inside the inner one, and comes out into another universe.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ and the charge radius is $r_q$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Squeeze a charge $Q$ onto a sphere of radius $\epsilon$ and its electric field stores the energy $Q^2/8\pi\epsilon_0\epsilon$, which grows without limit as the sphere shrinks, so a point electron ought to weigh infinitely much [arnowitt1962]. The classical theory of the electron had wanted a finite answer "since its inception", and the energy of the electron's own field "diverged linearly, with no realistic compensation possible" [arnowitt1962]. Could gravity be the compensation? Its energy is negative, and in 1960 Richard Arnowitt, Stanley Deser, and Charles Misner put the question to general relativity, with their own canonical formalism, built first for the free gravitational field [arnowitt1962, arnowitt1960prl, arnowitt1960].¶Their point was a shell: the charge and a bare mass $m_0$ spread over a sphere of radius $\epsilon$, which they then shrank to a point [arnowitt1962]. Gravity pulls on the total energy, by the principle of equivalence, so the binding energy is reckoned on the clothed mass $M$ itself, and $Mc^2 = m_0c^2 + Q^2/8\pi\epsilon_0\epsilon - GM^2/2\epsilon$ [arnowitt1962]. Solve for $M$, let $\epsilon$ go to zero, and the bare mass drops out: $M = |Q|/\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0G}$ [arnowitt1962]. The total mass, they reported, "becomes finite (although still quite large)", and "depends only on the charge and not on the bare mechanical mass" [arnowitt1960]. A particle with no charge ends up with no mass [arnowitt1962]. Two charges of the same sign weigh the sum of the two at any distance apart, their attraction cancelling their repulsion, and Achilles Papapetrou's static solution of 1947 is that balance [arnowitt1962, papapetrou1947].¶Arnowitt, Deser, and Misner's shell sat still [arnowitt1962]. What does it do once let go? One answer came in 1967 from V. de la Cruz and Werner Israel, for a shell of charged dust falling on a charged body at its centre [delacruz1967]. Another came in 1968 from Karel Kuchař, who integrated the equation of motion of a charged shell to a "law of conservation of energy" and read it "in full analogy with the special theory of relativity" [kuchar1968]. For dust of rest mass $m$ and charge $Q$ with flat space inside, it is $M = m\sqrt{1 + \dot{R}^2/c^2} + (Q^2/4\pi\epsilon_0 - Gm^2)/2c^2R$, with $R$ the radius of the shell, $\dot{R}$ its rate of change on the dust's own clock, and $M$ the mass in Hans Reissner and Gunnar Nordström's field outside [kuchar1968, gao2008, reissner1916, nordstrom1918]. Without the charge it is Israel's equation for the falling shell of dust [israel1966].¶With more charge than mass, $Q^2/4\pi\epsilon_0 > Gm^2$, the last term pushes outward, harder the smaller the shell, and a shell thrown in from far away stops at $R = (Q^2/4\pi\epsilon_0 - Gm^2)/2c^2(M - m)$ and turns round [gao2008]. Where the field outside is a black hole's, that radius lies inside both horizons [delacruz1967, gao2008]. How does a shell bounce out of a collapse that, seen from outside, is irreversible? De la Cruz and Israel called it an "apparent paradox" and explained it "in terms of the latticelike structure of the analytically extended Reissner-Nordström manifold" [delacruz1967]. That structure is John Graves and Dieter Brill's of 1960: the throat of a charged wormhole shrinks to a least radius and expands again, "cushioned" by the pressure of the electric field through it, and it does so periodically [graves1960]. The shell falls through both horizons of one outside world, turns, and climbs out through the horizons of the next [delacruz1967, gao2008].¶A shell of ordinary matter cannot use its charge to leave a singularity uncovered: David Boulware followed "the time development of a thin charged shell" in 1973 and found that a naked singularity needs matter of negative energy density [boulware1973]. The balanced shell, $Gm^2 = Q^2/4\pi\epsilon_0$, feels no net force, and $M = m$ at every radius [gao2008]. The theorem on it is Sijie Gao and José Lemos's, of 2008: such a shell "can only stay in neutral equilibrium outside its gravitational radius" [gao2008]. Its mass is that of Arnowitt, Deser, and Misner's point charge, and its field outside is the single hole of Sudhansu Datta Majumdar and Papapetrou [arnowitt1962, majumdar1947, papapetrou1947, hartle1972].¶De la Cruz and Israel raised "the possible relevance of the results to the problem of realistic gravitational collapse" [delacruz1967]. The way out runs through the inner horizon, a surface of infinite blueshift, Roger Penrose's observation of 1968 [penrose1968, brady1999]. Light that falls in after the shell arrives there with unbounded blueshift, and with it the mass inside the hole grows without limit at that horizon, which is Eric Poisson and Israel's mass inflation of 1989 [poisson1989]. Israel was an author of both papers, the bounce through the inner horizon in 1967 and its instability twenty two years later [delacruz1967, poisson1989].

related.text: The outside of the shell, with the mass and the charge of the shell for its two lengths. A shell with more charge than rest mass crosses both of its horizons and turns round inside the inner one [delacruz1967].
The inside of the shell, which encloses no charge and no mass. It stays flat from the fall through the turn to the way out.
The shell with no charge. At $r_q = 0$ the field outside is Schwarzschild's, nothing pushes back, and the shell falls to the centre [israel1966].
The shell of charged light, the limit $\mu \to 0$ of the charged dust at a fixed mass and charge outside. Its turning radius $r_q^2/r_s$ is the limit of the dust's [ori1991charged].

Charges at rest because their electric repulsion cancels their gravity. The balanced shell, $\mu = r_q = r_s/2$, has Majumdar and Papapetrou's single hole for its outside [arnowitt1962, papapetrou1947].

What becomes of the inner horizon the shell crosses on its way out. With radiation falling in behind the collapse, Eric Poisson and Werner Israel found the mass function growing without limit there [poisson1989].
The balanced shell filled in: dust whose charge density equals its mass density all through a ball, at rest at any radius, with the same extremal field outside [bonnor1965].

coordinates.name: Flat Interior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Charge radius of the charge $Q$ on the shell, $r_q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$; for $r_q < r_s/2$ the field outside has the horizons $r_\pm = r_s/2 \pm \sqrt{r_s^2/4 - r_q^2}$
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu < r_q$ and $\mu < r_s/2$ falls in from infinity and turns back at $R = (r_q^2 - \mu^2)/(r_s - 2\mu)$
Areal radius of the shell, a length. With $\tau$ the proper time of the dust and $\gamma = r_s/2\mu - (r_q^2 - \mu^2)/2\mu R$, it moves as $(dR/d(c\tau))^2 = \gamma^2 - 1$ while $dT/d\tau = \gamma$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, r, \theta, \phi)$ inside the shell, with $T$ the time of an observer at rest at the centre, carrying dimensions of time, and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Reissner-Nordström Exterior
domains: r = r_\pm \;\text{(the horizons, for}\; r_q < r_s/2\text{)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Charge radius of the charge $Q$ on the shell, $r_q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$; for $r_q < r_s/2$ the field outside has the horizons $r_\pm = r_s/2 \pm \sqrt{r_s^2/4 - r_q^2}$
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu < r_q$ and $\mu < r_s/2$ falls in from infinity and turns back at $R = (r_q^2 - \mu^2)/(r_s - 2\mu)$

Areal radius of the shell, a length. With $\tau$ the proper time of the dust, $\beta = r_s/2\mu - (r_q^2 + \mu^2)/2\mu R$, and $f = 1 - r_s/R + r_q^2/R^2$, it moves as $(dR/d(c\tau))^2 = \beta^2 - f$ while $f\,dt/d\tau = \beta$, and it reaches a horizon only as $t \to \pm\infty$

coordinates.convention: We use Reissner-Nordström's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ outside the shell, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, the same $r$ as inside. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(r_s\,r - 2r_q^2\right)\left(r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2\right)}{2r^5}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r_s\,r - 2r_q^2}{2r\left(r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2}{r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{r}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein Exterior
domains: r = r_\pm \;\text{(the horizons, for}\; r_q < r_s/2\text{)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Charge radius of the charge $Q$ on the shell, $r_q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$; for $r_q < r_s/2$ the field outside has the horizons $r_\pm = r_s/2 \pm \sqrt{r_s^2/4 - r_q^2}$
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu < r_q$ and $\mu < r_s/2$ falls in from infinity and turns back at $R = (r_q^2 - \mu^2)/(r_s - 2\mu)$

Areal radius of the shell, a length. With $\tau$ the proper time of the dust and $\beta = r_s/2\mu - (r_q^2 + \mu^2)/2\mu R$, it moves as $dv/d(c\tau) = 1/\left(\beta - dR/d(c\tau)\right)$, in through $r_+$ and $r_-$ to its turn, and back to $r_-$ as $v \to \infty$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$ outside the shell, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, constant along ingoing light rays, $r$ the areal radius, and $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r + r_q^2/r^2\right)^{-1}$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(r_s\,r - 2r_q^2\right)\left(r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2\right)}{2r^5}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{r_s\,r - 2r_q^2}{r^3}\dot{v}\dot{r} - \dfrac{r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2}{r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{r}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein Exterior
domains: r = r_\pm \;\text{(the horizons, for}\; r_q < r_s/2\text{)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Charge radius of the charge $Q$ on the shell, $r_q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$; for $r_q < r_s/2$ the field outside has the horizons $r_\pm = r_s/2 \pm \sqrt{r_s^2/4 - r_q^2}$
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu < r_q$ and $\mu < r_s/2$ falls in from infinity and turns back at $R = (r_q^2 - \mu^2)/(r_s - 2\mu)$

Areal radius of the shell, a length. With $\tau$ the proper time of the dust and $\beta = r_s/2\mu - (r_q^2 + \mu^2)/2\mu R$, it moves as $du/d(c\tau) = 1/\left(\beta + dR/d(c\tau)\right)$, from $r_-$ at $u \to -\infty$ to its turn, and out through $r_-$ and $r_+$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$ outside the shell, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, constant along outgoing light rays, $r$ the areal radius, and $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r + r_q^2/r^2\right)^{-1}$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(r_s\,r - 2r_q^2\right)\left(r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2\right)}{2r^5}\dot{u}^2 + \dfrac{r_s\,r - 2r_q^2}{r^3}\dot{u}\dot{r} - \dfrac{r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2}{r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r^2 - r_s\,r + r_q^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{r}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Isotropic Exterior

parameters.description: Length $a = r_s/4 + r_q/2$, with $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ the Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell and $r_q$ the charge radius of its charge $Q$, $r_q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$
Length $b = r_s/4 - r_q/2$, zero for the extreme field $r_q = r_s/2$, where the metric is that of Majumdar and Papapetrou's single hole
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu < r_q$ and $\mu < r_s/2$ falls in from infinity and turns back at $R = (r_q^2 - \mu^2)/(r_s - 2\mu)$
Isotropic radius of the shell, a length, where its areal radius is $R = (\epsilon + a)(\epsilon + b)/\epsilon$. A shell at rest there has the rest mass $\mu = a + b + 2ab/\epsilon$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi)$ outside the shell, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ the isotropic radius, a length, at which the areal radius is $r = (\rho + a)(\rho + b)/\rho$. The lengths $a = r_s/4 + r_q/2$ and $b = r_s/4 - r_q/2$ stand for the mass and the charge. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
